17215-rembrandt:
Mortimer Menpes made this 1905 Rembrandt book with an essay on the painter's life and work by C. Lewis Hind. Chapters cover the men who recovered Rembrandt's fame, the appeal of his paintings and etchings, epochs in his life, and the great triumvirate of his art. Sixteen plates, printed at the Menpes Press, show a Slav prince, a rabbi, the Holy Family, Titus in a red cap, and the Descent from the Cross.

Hind opens by asking a London businessman to imagine Rembrandt's absorption in art as keen as his own love of golf. The result is a short, warm guide for general readers. Art lovers will find a handsome, plain introduction to a painter whose light and shadow still draw crowds.
20607-rembrandt:
Rembrandt introduces the Dutch master's paintings through a set of chosen plates and studies. Rembrandt painted his wife Saskia again and again, and those portraits are spread through the world's great galleries. The book guides readers from the famous canvases to the neglected ones.

One portrait of Saskia, kept at the Brera in Milan, is not so well known as most. On that account it is reproduced here. The commentary follows Rembrandt's light and shadow across portraits, Bible scenes, and self-portraits. It is a doorway book, meant to send readers to the galleries with sharper eyes.
32919-renshaw-fanning-s-quest-a-tale-of-:
Bertram Mitford's tale of the high veldt opens with a riding pair in earnest talk, a bright-faced young woman warning her companion that she would soon become his ruin. The man answers in dead earnest that he cannot accept it. Her horse grows restive under his spur, and the scene, half mocking and half rueful, sets a romance against open country and hard riding. The quest of the title will test both of them.

Renshaw Fanning's search carries him across the high veldt, where Mitford's frontier world of farms, horsemen, and old scores gives the love story its stakes. The novel mixes adventure with feeling, letting landscape and danger sharpen a courtship that begins in warning. It is a colonial romance of its period, brisk, outdoor, and fond of the country it describes.
9100-my-double-life-the-memoirs-of-sarah:
Sarah Bernhardt, the great French actress, told her life in these memoirs, published in London in 1907 with many portraits. From childhood and boarding school to convent life, her debut, and her rise on the Paris stage, she recalls teachers, rivals, and the fierce will that made her famous. The title hints at her two lives, on stage and off.

Bernhardt writes with flair and frankness, sparing neither herself nor the theater world around her. Readers meet the young girl who became the Divine Sarah, adored across Europe and America. The memoirs remain a vivid self-portrait of a star who shaped what it meant to act.
britannica-1911-carlstadt:
Carlstadt (1480–1541) was a German reformer. His real name was Andreas Rudolf Bodenstein. This long 1911 Britannica entry traces his career. He was born at Carlstadt, in Bohemia, as the entry states. He entered the university of Erfurt in 1499. He moved to Cologne in 1503, and then to Wittenberg. At Wittenberg he built a name as a teacher of philosophy. He championed the scholastic system of Thomas Aquinas there.

In 1510 Carlstadt became doctor of theology and archdeacon. In 1513 he was made ordinary professor of theology. He went to Rome in 1515 to study law. The papal city worked on him as it had on Luther. He returned in 1516 an opponent of Thomist teaching. He now held the Augustinian doctrine of grace alone. His 151 theses of September 1516 are noted in the entry. The article follows his part in the early Reformation from there.
britannica-1911-freudenstadt: Freudenstadt is a town of Germany, in the kingdom of Württemberg, on the right bank of the Murg, 40 miles south-west of Stuttgart on the railway to Hochdorf. It has about 7000 people, a Protestant and a Roman Catholic church, and small works making cloth, furniture, knives, nails, and glass. Visitors come for its air as a climatic health resort. The town was founded in 1599 by Protestant refugees from Salzburg. The hosted file also holds the neighbouring entries for Fresno, Fresnoy, Fret, and Freund.
britannica-1911-kronstadt:
Kronstadt, or Cronstadt, is a strongly fortified seaport town of Russia. It is the chief naval station of the Russian fleet in the northern seas and the seat of the Russian admiralty. It stands on the island of Kotlin, near the head of the Gulf of Finland, 20 miles W. of St Petersburg, whose chief port it is. Its people numbered 45,115 in 1867 and 59,539 in 1897.

The old forts that defied the Anglo-French fleets in the Crimean War now count for less. From Todleben's plans a new fort, Constantine, and four batteries rose between 1856 and 1871 to guard the main approach, with seven more batteries on the shallow northern channel. All are low, thick earthworks with heavy Krupp guns in turrets. The island splits the sea road to St Petersburg into two channels, and a canal cut in 1875–1885, 23 feet deep, eased the way through the shallows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armenierstadt:
Armenierstadt, in Hungarian Szamos-Ujvar and Latin Armenopolis, is a city in Transylvania's Szolnok-Doboka county on the upper Szamos, an eastern branch of the Theiss. It is the home of a Uniat Greek diocese, Armenopolis, covering northern Transylvania. That see answers to Fogaras and Alba Julia's archbishop, resident at Blasendorf. The city was established about 1700 by Armenians who had emigrated from Armenia early in the fourteenth century and first settled on the Krim and Moldau banks.

In the seventeenth century they migrated to Transylvania, and after a two-year struggle led by Armenian-Catholic Bishop Auxentius Veerzereskul, they passed from Eutychianism, a teaching on Christ's nature, to Catholicism. Under the bull Ad Apostolicam Sedem of 26 November 1853 the city was made a diocese. Its first bishop Johann Alexi served from 1854 to 1865, followed by Vancsa, Pavel, and Johann Szabo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernhard-have:
Bernhard Havestadt, a German Jesuit missionary in Chile, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cologne in 1714, he died at Münster after 1778. He joined the Jesuits in 1732 and sailed to Chile in 1746, one of 102 German Jesuits who worked the Chilean mission between 1720 and 1767.

Twenty years among the Araucanian Indians, spent mostly in their country, showed remarkable energy. Gifted in languages, knowing nine more or less well, he threw himself into Chilidugu, the Araucanian tongue, which he said towered over other languages as the Andes tower over other mountains. His grammar and dictionary preserve that language for later study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-hoc:
Michael Ott's entry follows Conrad of Hochstadt, also Hostaden, Cologne Archbishop and Imperial Elector from 1238 to 1261. Son of Count Lothar and Mathilde of Vianden, he died on 28 September 1261. In 1216 he held Wevelinghoven parish near Düsseldorf as beneficiary. By 1226 he was Cologne cathedral canon, later provost. After Henry of Molenark died on 26 March 1238, the chapter elected him archbishop. Frederick II gave him insignia at Brescia that August, and Ludolf of Münster ordained and consecrated him on 28 October 1239.

Early months found him beside the emperor against Gregory IX, but he soon joined the papal party. Innocent made him legate in Germany on 14 March 1249, after Mainz Archbishop Sifrit's death left it vacant. At the new king's election he sold his vote to Richard of Cornwall, Henry III's brother. Crowning him at Aachen on 17 May 1257 was his last act. He lies in Cologne cathedral, whose cornerstone he laid on 15 August 1248.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-von:
Friedrich von Schmidt, a leading modern Gothic architect, built and restored some of the great churches of Austria and Germany. Born at Frickenhofen in 1825, he worked fifteen years on Cologne Cathedral, drawing most of the tower plans. After becoming a Catholic in 1858 he taught at Milan and restored San Ambrogio, then moved to Vienna as academy professor and cathedral architect.

At Vienna he rebuilt the spire of Saint Stephen's and designed the town hall, whose tall central tower rises 328 feet above a broad court. He also raised churches for Saint Lazarus, the White Tanners, and the Brigittines, and restored the cathedral at Fünfkirchen. His motto joined German force with Italian freedom, softening Gothic height with strong horizontal lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gilles-marie-:
Gilles-Marie Oppenordt, also called Oppenord, was a celebrated rococo artist born at Paris in 1672, who died there in 1742. Sent to Rome as a boy on a royal pension, he studied for eight years chiefly under Bernini and Borromini. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the French Borromini, a master of the Regency manner of salon and boudoir decoration.

With Robert de Cotte he shaped the rich rocaille border and shell ornament drawn from the Italian grotesque. The high altars of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and Saint-Sulpice won him the regent's favor, and he decorated the Palais Royal and the Hôtel du Grand Prieur. In 1721 the continuing work at Saint-Sulpice passed to him. He was also an unusual talent as a draughtsman, and his designs survive in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herman-von-ma:
Herman von Mallinckrodt, a German parliamentarian born at Minden in 1821, was raised Catholic by his mother though his father was Evangelical. He studied law at Berlin and Bonn and rose to government councillor at Düsseldorf. A transfer to Merseburg against his will led to his pensioning in 1872. Elected to the Prussian House in 1852, he helped found the Catholic Fraction defending church rights, later called the Centre, losing his mandate in the 1863 dissolution.

Returning to the Prussian Lower House in 1868, Mallinckrodt led the Centre Party from 1870 until his death, alongside the Reichensperger brothers and, after 1872, Windthorst. Colleagues praised his force, dignity, and prudence, and Falk, his antagonist as minister of worship, called him an honourable Centre member, a man who lived and fought for his convictions. Rising to his height in the Kulturkampf, he spoke last on 19 May 1874, closing with Per crucem ad lucem, and died days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-heinri:
Johann Heinrich Achterfeldt, a German theologian born at Wesel in 1788 and dead at Bonn in 1877, became Bonn theology professor in 1826. In 1832 he founded with Braun a journal for philosophy and Catholic theology whose chief aim was defending Hermes's teaching.

Achterfeldt also put out Hermes's teachings after his death as Christian-Catholic Dogmatics in 1834 to 1836, sparking sharp dispute until Gregory XVI put Hermes on the Index in September 1835. In 1843 Achterfeldt chose a ban over signing Cologne's required faith pledge. Hermesianism faded after 1848, yet he clung to it until restored in 1862 and fully cleared in 1873 after submission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maximilian-va:
Maximilian van der Sandt, also called Sandaus, was a Dutch Jesuit born at Amsterdam in 1578 who died at Cologne in 1656. He went into the Society of Jesus in 1597, taught philosophy at Wurzburg and Scripture at Mainz, and took charge of the Wurzburg episcopal seminary as its superior. He turned out many works on philosophy and theology.

His best-known piece took on the Batavian Calvinist Lawrence in defence of Jesuit moral teaching: the Castigatio conscientiae Jesuiticae cauteriata of 1617. People said of him that his seventy-eight years of life each left behind a book. Beside the polemics sit devotional treatises on the Blessed Virgin and many ascetical and mystical works. Short as the sketch is beside the man's vast output, Sommervogel and Poulain serve as guides to his bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pauline-malli:
Pauline Mallinckrodt was foundress of the Sisters of Christian Charity, born at Minden in Westphalia on 3 June 1817 and dead at Paderborn on 30 April 1881. Sister of Catholic political leader Hermann Mallinckrodt, she first ran a Paderborn blind institute and infant school. After her father's death she went to Paris to ask Mother Barat to take the blind institute under her congregation.

Prussia barred a French congregation, so Pauline founded the Sisters of Christian Charity on 21 August 1849 and became first superior. Pius IX approved the congregation on 21 February 1863. It grew so fast that before the Kulturkampf, which briefly crushed it, it counted twenty houses and 250 members across Germany. On 1 May 1873 its first sisters reached America, taking Saint Henry's school at New Orleans, and Pauline herself arrived on 7 June to plan a Wilkes-Barre mother-house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-joseph-:
Peter Joseph Arnoudt was a Belgian Jesuit writer on the Sacred Heart, born at Moere in 1811. He entered the Society at Florissant, Missouri, in 1831, taught in the Missouri province's colleges, and proved a finished Greek scholar. After ordination, a dangerous illness moved him to vow zealous labour for devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

On recovery he wrote De Imitatione Sacri Cordis Jesu and sent the manuscript to Rome in 1846, where it lay mislaid for ten years. Approved by Father General Roothaan, it appeared at Einsiedeln in 1863 and in English at Cincinnati in 1865. French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Flemish, and Hungarian versions followed, the French alone reaching eighteen editions by 1887. Unpublished Greek verse and ascetical writings survived him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Ingolstadt's university ran from 1472 to 1800 and was founded by Louis the Rich, Duke of Bavaria. Pope Pius II had granted the privileges of a studium generale with all four faculties on 7 April 1458, but unsettled times blocked their use. Modelled on Vienna, Ingolstadt aimed chiefly at furthering and spreading Christian belief. An unusually large endowment came from clergy and religious orders, and the Bishop of Eichstätt served as chancellor.

The formal inauguration took place on 26 June 1472, and 489 students matriculated in the first semester. As elsewhere before the sixteenth century, philosophy formed the broad base of study. The entry follows the university through its humanist age, its Jesuit period, and its later decline, closing with its removal to Landshut and then Munich, where its line continues today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wiener-neusta:
Wiener-Neustadt was a suppressed see in Lower Austria, erected by Paul II on 14 January 1469 at Frederick III's request and immediately subject to the Holy See. At first coterminous with the town of Wiener-Neustadt, it gained the new parish of Theresienfeld in 1769 and in 1784 extended its territory to Styria's boundary.

On 21 April 1785 Joseph II incorporated the see in Vienna's archdiocese. Its last bishop, Heinrich Johann Kerens, Jesuit, 1775 to 1785, with his cathedral chapter, was transferred to the newly erected diocese of St Pölten. Of its twenty-three bishops the most noteworthy were Melchior Klesl, also Bishop of Vienna and cardinal, 1614 to 1630. Leopold Count von Kollonitsch, 1670 to 1685, later Bishop of Raab, and Christopher Royas von Spinola, 1686 to 1695.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GinocchioGerald:
Gerald Ginocchio, a Wofford College sociologist, presented a conference paper with Dennis W. MacDonald on August 18, 1995. The paper, given to the Society for the Study of Social Problems in Washington, D.C., studies the Kennedy assassination as a failure of institutions. Its question is what such an event does to a society.

Sociology treats the assassination not as a puzzle of shots but as a stress test of public trust. Ginocchio and MacDonald argue the institutions meant to answer the event failed at the task. The paper preserves the academy taking up the case three decades on.
my-double-life-the-memoirs-of-sarah-bern:
Sarah Bernhardt tells her own life in these memoirs, issued in 1907. Heinemann published them in London, and Appleton in America. Portraits and pictures fill the volume. One shows her as Adrienne Lecouvreur, a famed stage role.

Bernhardt was the most famous actress of her age. Her double life joins the stage self and the private woman. The memoirs trace her rise, her art, and her fame. Ads in this edition praise Bram Stoker's life of Henry Irving too. Readers get a star's own account of the French theatre world she ruled for decades.
rembrandt:
Mortimer Menpes wrote this study of Rembrandt, with an essay on the painter's life and work by C. Lewis Hind. Adam and Charles Black of London published it in 1905. A front picture shows Rembrandt's Portrait of a Slav Prince of 1637, held at the Hermitage in St. Petersburg.

Four chapters are listed in the contents. The first treats the recoverers of Rembrandt, those who won back his fame. Two chapters then take up the appeal of the paintings and of the etchings in turn. A fourth covers epochs in Rembrandt's life, and a fifth chapter begins as the list breaks off. Menpes himself painted and etched, and writes as a working artist.
